FRONT: What does I/O redirection '>' do vs '>>'?
BACK: '>' redirects stdout to a file, overwriting it. '>>' appends to the file. Example: echo hello > file (overwrites), echo world >> file (appends).

FRONT: How do you redirect stderr separately from stdout?
BACK: 2> redirects stderr. Example: find / -name '*.conf' 2>/dev/null discards errors. 2>> appends stderr. 2>&1 merges stderr into stdout.

FRONT: How do you redirect both stdout and stderr to the same file?
BACK: command &> file (bash shorthand) or command > file 2>&1 (portable). The order matters — 2>&1 must come after > to work correctly.

FRONT: What does the pipe operator '|' do?
BACK: Connects stdout of the left command to stdin of the right command. Example: ps aux | grep httpd | wc -l counts httpd processes.

FRONT: What does the tee command do?
BACK: Reads from stdin and writes to both stdout and a file simultaneously. Example: echo hello | tee file.txt writes to file.txt AND displays on screen. Use tee -a to append.

FRONT: How do you use grep to search for a pattern in files?
BACK: grep PATTERN FILE. Key flags: -i (case-insensitive), -r (recursive), -n (line numbers), -v (invert match), -c (count matches), -l (filenames only).

FRONT: How do you use extended regular expressions with grep?
BACK: grep -E or egrep. Enables +, ?, |, (), {} without escaping. Example: grep -E 'error|warning|fail' /var/log/messages.

FRONT: What are the most useful regex anchors and quantifiers?
BACK: ^ (start of line), $ (end of line), . (any char), * (zero or more), + (one or more, extended), ? (zero or one, extended), [] (character class), [^] (negated class).

FRONT: How do you SSH to a remote system?
BACK: ssh user@hostname. Use -p PORT for non-standard port. Use -i KEYFILE for a specific private key. First connection prompts to accept the host key fingerprint.

FRONT: How do you copy files to/from a remote system with scp?
BACK: scp file user@host:/path (local→remote). scp user@host:/path file (remote→local). scp -r for directories. sftp user@host provides an interactive FTP-like session.

FRONT: What is the difference between su and su -?
BACK: su switches user but keeps the current environment (PATH, HOME, etc.). su - (or su -l) does a full login shell, loading the target user's environment. Always prefer su - for consistent behavior.

FRONT: How do you run a command as another user?
BACK: sudo command runs as root. sudo -u USER command runs as a specific user. sudo -i opens a root login shell. sudo -s opens a root shell keeping the current environment.

FRONT: How do you create an archive with tar?
BACK: tar cf archive.tar files — creates an archive. Add -v for verbose. Key: c=create, f=filename. Example: tar cf /tmp/backup.tar /etc creates a tarball of /etc.

FRONT: How do you extract a tar archive?
BACK: tar xf archive.tar — extracts to current directory. tar xf archive.tar -C /target — extracts to /target. Key: x=extract.

FRONT: How do you compress/decompress with tar using gzip vs bzip2?
BACK: tar czf file.tar.gz (gzip, faster). tar cjf file.tar.bz2 (bzip2, smaller). For extraction: tar xzf and tar xjf respectively. The z/j flag selects the compressor.

FRONT: How do you preserve SELinux contexts and ACLs with tar?
BACK: tar --selinux --acls --xattrs -czf backup.tar.gz /path. Critical for RHCSA — without these flags, restoring files loses security labels and extended attributes.

FRONT: What are the essential vim commands for the RHCSA?
BACK: i (insert mode), Esc (normal mode), :w (save), :q (quit), :wq (save+quit), :q! (force quit), dd (delete line), yy (yank line), p (paste), u (undo), /pattern (search), :set nu (line numbers).

FRONT: How do you create, delete, copy, and move files?
BACK: touch file (create/update timestamp), cp src dst (copy, -r for dirs, -a to preserve all attributes), mv src dst (move/rename), rm file (delete, -r for dirs, -f to force).

FRONT: How do you create and remove directories?
BACK: mkdir dir (create). mkdir -p path/to/deep/dir (create parent dirs as needed). rmdir dir (remove empty dir). rm -rf dir (remove dir and all contents — dangerous).

FRONT: What is a hard link and how do you create one?
BACK: A hard link is an additional directory entry pointing to the same inode. Created with ln target linkname. Both names are equal — deleting one leaves the other intact. Cannot cross filesystems. Cannot link directories.

FRONT: What is a soft (symbolic) link and how do you create one?
BACK: A soft link is a file containing a path to another file. Created with ln -s target linkname. Can cross filesystems and link directories. Breaks if the target is deleted (dangling link).

FRONT: What is the key difference between hard and soft links?
BACK: Hard links share the same inode number (ls -i shows this). Soft links have their own inode pointing to a pathname. Hard links survive target rename/move; soft links break. Hard links can't cross filesystems; soft links can.

FRONT: How do you set permissions with chmod using symbolic notation?
BACK: chmod u+x file (owner +execute). chmod go-w file (group/others -write). chmod a=r file (all=read only). u=user, g=group, o=others, a=all. Operators: + (add), - (remove), = (set exactly).

FRONT: How do you set permissions with chmod using octal notation?
BACK: chmod 755 file → rwxr-xr-x. Each digit: r=4, w=2, x=1, sum them. 7=rwx, 6=rw-, 5=r-x, 4=r--, 0=---. Three digits: owner, group, others.

FRONT: How do you change file ownership?
BACK: chown user file (change owner). chown user:group file (change both). chown :group file (change group only). chgrp group file (change group). Add -R for recursive.

FRONT: What are SUID, SGID, and sticky bit?
BACK: SUID (4xxx or u+s): file runs as owner, not caller (e.g., /usr/bin/passwd). SGID (2xxx or g+s): file runs as group; on dirs, new files inherit the dir's group. Sticky (1xxx or o+t): on dirs, only file owner can delete (e.g., /tmp).

FRONT: How do you use the man command effectively?
BACK: man COMMAND shows the manual. man -k KEYWORD (or apropos) searches all man pages. Man sections: 1=commands, 5=file formats, 8=admin commands. Example: man 5 passwd shows the passwd file format, not the command.

FRONT: Where is system documentation stored besides man pages?
BACK: info COMMAND (GNU texinfo docs, more detailed than man). /usr/share/doc/ contains package documentation, READMEs, example configs, and changelogs. Use rpm -qd PACKAGE to list a package's doc files.

FRONT: How do you use the find command?
BACK: find PATH OPTIONS. Examples: find / -name '*.conf' (by name), find /home -user bob (by owner), find / -perm -4000 (SUID files), find /tmp -mtime +7 (modified >7 days ago), find / -size +100M (large files).

FRONT: How do you use find with -exec?
BACK: find /path -name '*.log' -exec rm {} \; (runs rm on each match). Use {} as placeholder for the found file. Use \; to terminate the command. Use + instead of \; to batch files for efficiency.

FRONT: What do head, tail, wc, sort, cut, and uniq do?
BACK: head -n 5 (first 5 lines), tail -n 5 (last 5), tail -f (follow live output). wc -l (count lines). sort (alphabetical, -n numeric, -r reverse). cut -d: -f1 (extract field 1, delimiter :). uniq (remove adjacent duplicates, use with sort).

FRONT: How do you configure a DNF/YUM repository?
BACK: Create a .repo file in /etc/yum.repos.d/ with [repo-id], name=, baseurl= (or mirrorlist=), enabled=1, gpgcheck=1, gpgkey=. Or use dnf config-manager --add-repo URL.

FRONT: What are the essential dnf commands for package management?
BACK: dnf install PKG, dnf remove PKG, dnf update (update all), dnf search KEYWORD, dnf info PKG, dnf list installed, dnf list available, dnf provides FILE (which package owns a file), dnf repolist.

FRONT: How do you work with DNF package groups?
BACK: dnf group list (show available groups). dnf group install 'Group Name' (install all packages in a group). dnf group remove 'Group Name'. dnf group info 'Group Name' (see what's included).

FRONT: How do you view and undo DNF transaction history?
BACK: dnf history (list transactions). dnf history info ID (details of a transaction). dnf history undo ID (reverse a transaction). Useful for rolling back accidental installs or removals.

FRONT: How do you import a GPG key for a repository?
BACK: rpm --import URL_OR_FILE imports the key. dnf does this automatically if gpgkey= is set in the .repo file and you confirm on first install. List imported keys: rpm -qa gpg-pubkey*.

FRONT: How do you install a local RPM file with dnf?
BACK: dnf localinstall package.rpm (older syntax) or simply dnf install ./package.rpm. dnf resolves and installs dependencies from configured repos automatically, unlike plain rpm -i.

FRONT: How do you add a Flatpak remote repository?
BACK: flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists NAME URL. Example: flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo. List remotes: flatpak remotes.

FRONT: How do you install and manage Flatpak applications?
BACK: flatpak install REMOTE APP_ID (install). flatpak remove APP_ID (uninstall). flatpak list (show installed). flatpak update (update all). flatpak run APP_ID (launch). flatpak search KEYWORD (search remote).

FRONT: How is Flatpak different from RPM packages?
BACK: Flatpak apps are sandboxed (use kernel namespaces and seccomp), bundle their own dependencies (no library conflicts), and are distributed via OSTree repos. RPM packages install system-wide and share libraries. Flatpak is for desktop apps; RPM is for system software.

FRONT: What is a bash shebang line and why does it matter?
BACK: #!/bin/bash as the first line tells the kernel which interpreter to use. Without it, the script may run in sh (missing bash features). Always include it. Make the script executable: chmod +x script.sh.

FRONT: How does an if/then/else statement work in bash?
BACK: if CONDITION; then COMMANDS; elif CONDITION; then COMMANDS; else COMMANDS; fi. Condition is usually test or [ ]. Example: if [ -f /etc/hosts ]; then echo exists; else echo missing; fi

FRONT: What is the difference between test, [ ], and [[ ]]?
BACK: test and [ ] are equivalent ([ is a command, ] closes it). [[ ]] is a bash keyword with extra features: pattern matching (=~), no word splitting, && and || operators. For RHCSA, [ ] is standard and sufficient.

FRONT: What are the common file test operators in bash?
BACK: -f FILE (is regular file), -d FILE (is directory), -e FILE (exists), -r FILE (readable), -w FILE (writable), -x FILE (executable), -s FILE (exists and non-empty), -L FILE (is symlink).

FRONT: What are the bash integer comparison operators?
BACK: -eq (equal), -ne (not equal), -gt (greater than), -lt (less than), -ge (greater or equal), -le (less or equal). Used inside [ ]: if [ $count -gt 10 ]; then echo big; fi

FRONT: What are the bash string comparison operators?
BACK: = or == (equal), != (not equal), -z STRING (is empty), -n STRING (is non-empty). Always quote variables: if [ "$var" = "hello" ]. Without quotes, empty variables cause syntax errors.

FRONT: How do you write a for loop in bash?
BACK: for VAR in LIST; do COMMANDS; done. Examples: for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; done. for file in /etc/*.conf; do wc -l "$file"; done. for user in $(cat users.txt); do useradd $user; done.

FRONT: How do you write a while loop in bash?
BACK: while CONDITION; do COMMANDS; done. Example: while read line; do echo "$line"; done < /etc/passwd. Use break to exit early, continue to skip to next iteration.

FRONT: What are positional parameters in a bash script?
BACK: $0 (script name), $1-$9 (arguments 1-9), ${10}+ (10+). $@ (all arguments as separate words), $* (all as one string), $# (argument count). Example: ./script.sh hello world → $1=hello, $2=world, $#=2.

FRONT: How do you use command substitution in bash?
BACK: $(command) captures a command's stdout as a string. Example: today=$(date +%F) stores the date. count=$(wc -l < /etc/passwd) counts lines. Older syntax uses backticks `command` but $() is preferred (nestable, more readable).

FRONT: What is $? and how do you use exit codes?
BACK: $? holds the exit code of the last command. 0 = success, non-zero = failure. Use in scripts: if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then echo failed; fi. Set your own: exit 0 (success) or exit 1 (failure) at end of script.

FRONT: How do you process command output in a script?
BACK: Use command substitution or pipes. Example: for pid in $(pgrep httpd); do echo "Process: $pid"; done. Or: df -h | grep '/dev/sd' | while read line; do echo $line; done.

FRONT: How do you use read to get user input in a script?
BACK: read -p 'Enter name: ' name captures input into variable $name. read -s for silent input (passwords). read -t 5 for 5-second timeout. Example: read -p 'Continue? (y/n): ' answer; if [ "$answer" = y ]; then ...

FRONT: How do you start, stop, and restart a service with systemctl?
BACK: systemctl start SERVICE (start now). systemctl stop SERVICE (stop now). systemctl restart SERVICE (stop then start). systemctl reload SERVICE (reload config without full restart, if supported).

FRONT: How do you enable a service to start at boot?
BACK: systemctl enable SERVICE (start at boot). systemctl disable SERVICE (don't start at boot). systemctl enable --now SERVICE (enable AND start immediately). These create/remove symlinks in /etc/systemd/system/.

FRONT: How do you check the status of a service?
BACK: systemctl status SERVICE shows: active/inactive, enabled/disabled, recent log lines, PID, memory usage, and the cgroup. systemctl is-active SERVICE and systemctl is-enabled SERVICE return just the state.

FRONT: What does systemctl mask do?
BACK: systemctl mask SERVICE creates a symlink to /dev/null, preventing the service from being started by any means (manual, dependency, or boot). systemctl unmask SERVICE removes it. Stronger than disable.

FRONT: How do you list all services and their states?
BACK: systemctl list-units --type=service (running units). systemctl list-unit-files --type=service (all installed, shows enabled/disabled/masked). Add --state=running or --state=failed to filter.

FRONT: What are the four main systemd boot targets?
BACK: multi-user.target (text mode, networked, most servers). graphical.target (GUI desktop). rescue.target (single-user, root shell, basic system). emergency.target (minimal, root shell, root filesystem read-only).

FRONT: How do you change the default boot target?
BACK: systemctl set-default TARGET. Example: systemctl set-default multi-user.target. Verify with systemctl get-default. This creates a symlink at /etc/systemd/system/default.target.

FRONT: How do you switch to a different target at runtime?
BACK: systemctl isolate TARGET. Example: systemctl isolate rescue.target drops to rescue mode immediately. Only targets with AllowIsolate=yes can be isolated.

FRONT: How do you interrupt the boot process to reset the root password?
BACK: 1) Reboot, edit GRUB entry (press 'e'), append rd.break to the linux line. 2) Ctrl+x to boot. 3) mount -o remount,rw /sysroot. 4) chroot /sysroot. 5) passwd root. 6) touch /.autorelabel (for SELinux). 7) exit twice.

FRONT: Why is touch /.autorelabel needed after a root password reset?
BACK: The chroot environment bypasses SELinux. The new /etc/shadow file gets an incorrect SELinux label. /.autorelabel tells SELinux to relabel the entire filesystem on next boot, fixing the context. Without it, you can't log in.

FRONT: How do you edit the GRUB kernel command line at boot?
BACK: At the GRUB menu, press 'e' to edit the selected entry. Navigate to the 'linux' line and append parameters (rd.break, systemd.unit=rescue.target, etc.). Press Ctrl+x to boot with changes. These changes are temporary (one boot only).

FRONT: How do you identify CPU/memory-intensive processes?
BACK: top (interactive, press M to sort by memory, P by CPU, k to kill). ps aux --sort=-%mem (sort by memory). ps aux --sort=-%cpu (sort by CPU). Or use pidof/pgrep to find specific processes.

FRONT: How do you kill a process?
BACK: kill PID (sends SIGTERM, graceful). kill -9 PID (SIGKILL, forced, cannot be caught). kill -15 PID (SIGTERM explicitly). killall NAME (kill by name). pkill PATTERN (kill by pattern). Always try SIGTERM before SIGKILL.

FRONT: What is the difference between nice and renice?
BACK: nice -n VALUE COMMAND starts a new process with adjusted priority. renice -n VALUE -p PID changes priority of a running process. Range: -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). Only root can set negative nice values.

FRONT: What is tuned and how do you manage tuning profiles?
BACK: tuned is a daemon that applies system tuning profiles for different workloads. tuned-adm list (show profiles), tuned-adm active (current profile), tuned-adm profile NAME (switch), tuned-adm recommend (suggested profile).

FRONT: What are common tuned profiles?
BACK: throughput-performance (max throughput, servers). latency-performance (low latency). virtual-guest (optimized for VMs). virtual-host (optimized for hypervisors). balanced (compromise). powersave (energy saving). network-latency (low network latency).

FRONT: How do you use journalctl to view system logs?
BACK: journalctl (all logs). journalctl -u SERVICE (specific unit). journalctl -p err (priority: emerg/alert/crit/err/warning/notice/info/debug). journalctl -f (follow live). journalctl -b (current boot). journalctl -b -1 (previous boot).

FRONT: How do you filter journalctl by time?
BACK: journalctl --since '2024-01-15 10:00:00' --until '2024-01-15 12:00:00'. Shortcuts: --since yesterday, --since today, --since '1 hour ago'. Combine with -u and -p for precise filtering.

FRONT: How do you make the systemd journal persistent across reboots?
BACK: mkdir -p /var/log/journal && systemctl restart systemd-journald. Or set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf and restart the service. Without this, logs are stored in /run/log/journal/ (tmpfs, lost on reboot).

FRONT: What are the important log files in /var/log/?
BACK: /var/log/messages (general system log), /var/log/secure (auth/sudo), /var/log/boot.log (boot messages), /var/log/cron (cron jobs), /var/log/maillog (mail), /var/log/dnf.log (package manager). Most are now also accessible via journalctl.

FRONT: How do you use lsblk and blkid?
BACK: lsblk shows block devices in a tree: name, size, type, mountpoint. lsblk -f adds filesystem type, label, UUID. blkid shows UUID, TYPE, LABEL for block devices. Both are essential for identifying disks before partitioning.

FRONT: How do you create a GPT partition with fdisk?
BACK: fdisk /dev/sdX → g (create GPT table, if new disk) → n (new partition) → accept or set partition number, first sector, size (+500M, +2G, etc.) → t (change type: 8e for LVM, 82 for swap) → w (write and exit). Run partprobe after.

FRONT: What does partprobe do?
BACK: partprobe informs the kernel of partition table changes without rebooting. Run it after fdisk/gdisk/parted to make the kernel re-read the partition table. Without it, the kernel may not see new partitions until reboot.

FRONT: What is LVM and what are PVs, VGs, and LVs?
BACK: LVM (Logical Volume Manager) provides flexible disk management. Physical Volumes (PVs): partitions/disks initialized for LVM. Volume Groups (VGs): pools of PVs. Logical Volumes (LVs): virtual partitions carved from VGs, easily resized.

FRONT: How do you create and inspect physical volumes?
BACK: pvcreate /dev/sdb1 (initialize a partition as PV). pvs (short summary). pvdisplay (detailed). pvremove /dev/sdb1 (remove PV label). The partition type should be set to 8e (Linux LVM) with fdisk.

FRONT: How do you create and manage volume groups?
BACK: vgcreate myvg /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 (create VG from PVs). vgs (summary). vgdisplay (detailed). vgextend myvg /dev/sdd1 (add a PV to existing VG). vgreduce myvg /dev/sdd1 (remove a PV).

FRONT: How do you create a logical volume?
BACK: lvcreate -L 500M -n mylv myvg (500MB LV named 'mylv' in VG 'myvg'). -L for exact size (M, G, T). -l for extents (-l 100%FREE uses all remaining space). Then: mkfs.xfs /dev/myvg/mylv.

FRONT: How do you display and remove logical volumes?
BACK: lvs (summary of all LVs). lvdisplay (detailed). lvremove /dev/myvg/mylv (delete LV — data is lost). To cleanly remove LVM: umount → lvremove → vgremove → pvremove.

FRONT: How do you extend a logical volume?
BACK: lvextend -L +200M /dev/myvg/mylv (add 200MB). lvextend -l +100%FREE /dev/myvg/mylv (use all remaining VG space). After extending the LV, you MUST also grow the filesystem (xfs_growfs or resize2fs).

FRONT: What is the /etc/fstab file format?
BACK: Six fields: DEVICE MOUNTPOINT FSTYPE OPTIONS DUMP PASS. Example: UUID=abc-123 /data xfs defaults 0 0. DEVICE can be UUID=, LABEL=, or /dev/path. PASS: 0=no fsck, 1=root, 2=other filesystems.

FRONT: How do you mount a filesystem by UUID?
BACK: Get the UUID: blkid /dev/sdb1. Add to /etc/fstab: UUID=xxxx-xxxx /mnt/data xfs defaults 0 0. Then: mount -a (mount all fstab entries) or mount /mnt/data. UUID is preferred over device paths because it's persistent across reboots.

FRONT: Why should you run 'systemctl daemon-reload' after editing /etc/fstab?
BACK: systemd generates mount units from /etc/fstab at boot and when daemon-reload runs. Without it, systemd's mount units are stale and may not match fstab. Always run it after fstab changes, then mount -a to test.

FRONT: How do you add swap space to a system?
BACK: 1) Create partition (type 82) or LV. 2) mkswap /dev/sdX1 (format as swap). 3) swapon /dev/sdX1 (activate). 4) Add to /etc/fstab: UUID=xxx swap swap defaults 0 0. 5) Verify: swapon --show or free -h.

FRONT: How do you add a swap file instead of a partition?
BACK: dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=1024 (create 1GB file). chmod 600 /swapfile. mkswap /swapfile. swapon /swapfile. Add to fstab: /swapfile swap swap defaults 0 0.

FRONT: How do you create an XFS filesystem?
BACK: mkfs.xfs /dev/sdX1 or mkfs.xfs /dev/myvg/mylv. XFS cannot be shrunk, only grown. Use xfs_growfs /mountpoint to expand (note: takes the mount point, not the device). XFS is the default filesystem on RHEL.

FRONT: How do you create ext4 and VFAT filesystems?
BACK: mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdX1 (Linux general purpose). mkfs.vfat /dev/sdX1 (FAT32, for EFI or USB). ext4 can be grown (resize2fs) AND shrunk (must be unmounted first). VFAT has no ownership/permissions.

FRONT: How do you mount and unmount filesystems?
BACK: mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/point (mount). mount -o ro /dev/sdX1 /mnt (read-only). umount /mnt/point or umount /dev/sdX1 (unmount). Can't unmount if in use — use lsof /mnt or fuser -m /mnt to find what's using it.

FRONT: What are common mount options?
BACK: defaults (rw,suid,dev,exec,auto,nouser,async). ro (read-only). noexec (no execution of binaries). nosuid (ignore SUID bits). nodev (ignore device files). noatime (don't update access times). _netdev (wait for network before mount).

FRONT: How do you mount an NFS share?
BACK: mount -t nfs server:/export/share /mnt/nfs. For persistence in /etc/fstab: server:/export/share /mnt/nfs nfs _netdev 0 0. The _netdev option ensures the system waits for the network before attempting the mount.

FRONT: What is autofs and why use it?
BACK: autofs automatically mounts filesystems on demand when accessed and unmounts after idle timeout. Saves resources and avoids boot failures from unavailable NFS servers. Managed by the autofs service.

FRONT: How do you configure autofs?
BACK: 1) Install autofs: dnf install autofs. 2) Edit /etc/auto.master: /mnt/auto /etc/auto.shares. 3) Create /etc/auto.shares: data -rw,sync server:/export/data. 4) systemctl enable --now autofs. Access /mnt/auto/data to trigger mount.

FRONT: What is the difference between autofs direct and indirect maps?
BACK: Indirect: mount point is relative to a parent directory (auto.master: /mnt/auto /etc/auto.map → access /mnt/auto/key). Direct: mount point is absolute (auto.master: /- /etc/auto.direct → map: /mnt/data -opts server:/path).

FRONT: How do you extend an XFS filesystem after extending the LV?
BACK: lvextend -L +500M /dev/myvg/mylv && xfs_growfs /mountpoint. xfs_growfs takes the MOUNT POINT (not the device) and the filesystem must be mounted. XFS can only grow, never shrink.

FRONT: How do you extend an ext4 filesystem after extending the LV?
BACK: lvextend -L +500M /dev/myvg/mylv && resize2fs /dev/myvg/mylv. resize2fs takes the DEVICE (not mount point). Can be run online (mounted). To shrink: umount first, e2fsck -f, then resize2fs with smaller size.

FRONT: How do you diagnose file permission problems?
BACK: ls -la (check owner, group, permissions). stat FILE (detailed permissions, SELinux context). namei -l /path/to/file (check permissions of every directory in the path). Also check SELinux: ls -Z, audit log for AVC denials.

FRONT: How do you schedule a one-time task with at?
BACK: at TIME (then type commands, Ctrl+D to finish). Examples: at 3pm, at now + 30 minutes, at 10:00 2025-01-15. atq lists pending jobs. atrm JOB_NUMBER removes a job. Requires the atd service running.

FRONT: What is the crontab syntax?
BACK: Five fields: MINUTE(0-59) HOUR(0-23) DAY(1-31) MONTH(1-12) WEEKDAY(0-7, 0 and 7=Sunday). * means every. Example: 30 2 * * 1 /script.sh runs at 2:30 AM every Monday. crontab -e edits, crontab -l lists, crontab -r removes.

FRONT: What are cron special directories and strings?
BACK: /etc/cron.d/ (system cron files, include user field). /etc/cron.daily/, hourly/, weekly/, monthly/ (drop scripts here). Special strings in crontab: @reboot, @yearly, @monthly, @weekly, @daily, @hourly.

FRONT: How do you create a systemd timer unit?
BACK: Create two files: a .timer and matching .service. The .timer has [Timer] section with OnCalendar= or OnBootSec=. Example: OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00 (daily at 2:30 AM). Enable with systemctl enable --now mytimer.timer.

FRONT: What is the OnCalendar= syntax for systemd timers?
BACK: Format: DayOfWeek Year-Month-Day Hour:Minute:Second. Examples: *-*-* 14:00:00 (daily 2pm), Mon *-*-* 09:00:00 (Mondays 9am), *-*-01 00:00:00 (first of month). Use systemd-analyze calendar SPEC to validate.

FRONT: What does Persistent=true do in a systemd timer?
BACK: If the system was off when a timer should have fired, Persistent=true runs the task immediately on next boot to catch up. Without it, missed runs are simply skipped. Add under [Timer] in the .timer file.

FRONT: How do you configure time synchronization with chrony?
BACK: chrony is the default NTP client on RHEL. Config: /etc/chrony.conf (set server or pool lines). Commands: chronyc sources (show time sources), chronyc tracking (sync status). timedatectl shows current time settings and NTP status.

FRONT: How do you use timedatectl?
BACK: timedatectl (show current settings). timedatectl set-timezone America/New_York. timedatectl set-ntp true (enable NTP via chronyd). timedatectl list-timezones (list all zones). timedatectl set-time '2024-01-15 10:30:00' (manual, NTP must be off).

FRONT: How do you install packages from the local filesystem or a remote repo?
BACK: dnf install ./package.rpm (local RPM). dnf install https://example.com/package.rpm (remote). dnf install --enablerepo=REPO package (specific repo). For Red Hat CDN: register with subscription-manager register, then dnf install.

FRONT: How do you modify the GRUB bootloader?
BACK: Edit /etc/default/grub (GRUB_TIMEOUT, GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX for kernel parameters). Then regenerate: grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg (BIOS) or grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/efi/EFI/redhat/grub.cfg (UEFI). Changes persist across kernel updates.

FRONT: What are useful GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX parameters?
BACK: systemd.unit=rescue.target (boot to rescue), rd.break (break into initramfs), console=ttyS0,115200 (serial console), selinux=0 (disable SELinux, not recommended), net.ifnames=0 (legacy NIC names).

FRONT: How do you configure a static IP with nmcli?
BACK: nmcli con add type ethernet con-name myconn ifname eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.100/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8 ipv4.method manual. Then: nmcli con up myconn.

FRONT: How do you modify an existing NetworkManager connection?
BACK: nmcli con mod CONN_NAME ipv4.addresses 10.0.0.50/24. nmcli con mod CONN_NAME ipv4.dns '8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4'. nmcli con mod CONN_NAME +ipv4.dns 1.1.1.1 (append). After changes: nmcli con up CONN_NAME to apply.

FRONT: How do you configure IPv6 with nmcli?
BACK: nmcli con mod CONN ipv6.addresses 'fd00::1/64' ipv6.method manual. Or ipv6.method auto for SLAAC. nmcli con up CONN to apply. Verify: ip -6 addr show.

FRONT: How do you show and manage NetworkManager connections and devices?
BACK: nmcli con show (list all connections, active marked). nmcli con show CONN (detailed settings). nmcli dev status (list devices and states). nmcli con up CONN (activate). nmcli con down CONN (deactivate).

FRONT: How do you view IP addresses and routes?
BACK: ip addr show (or ip a) shows all interfaces and addresses. ip route show (or ip r) shows routing table. ip -6 addr for IPv6. ip link show for interface state (up/down). ip addr show dev eth0 for specific interface.

FRONT: How do you set the system hostname?
BACK: hostnamectl set-hostname newname.example.com (persistent). hostnamectl (show current). hostname (show short name). The hostname is stored in /etc/hostname. Also update /etc/hosts with the new name for local resolution.

FRONT: How do you configure hostname resolution?
BACK: /etc/hosts (static mappings, checked first). /etc/resolv.conf (DNS servers — managed by NetworkManager, don't edit directly). Set DNS via nmcli con mod CONN ipv4.dns. /etc/nsswitch.conf controls resolution order (files dns).

FRONT: How do you manage firewalld zones?
BACK: firewall-cmd --get-zones (list all). firewall-cmd --get-default-zone (show default). firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=ZONE (change default). firewall-cmd --get-active-zones (zones with assigned interfaces). Common zones: public (default), trusted, block, drop.

FRONT: How do you add services and ports in firewalld?
BACK: firewall-cmd --add-service=http (runtime only). firewall-cmd --add-service=http --permanent (survives reboot). firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent. After --permanent changes: firewall-cmd --reload. List: firewall-cmd --list-all.

FRONT: How do you remove firewall rules?
BACK: firewall-cmd --remove-service=http --permanent. firewall-cmd --remove-port=8080/tcp --permanent. firewall-cmd --reload. Always use --permanent and --reload together for persistent changes.

FRONT: How do you list all firewall rules and available services?
BACK: firewall-cmd --list-all (current zone's rules). firewall-cmd --list-all --zone=ZONE (specific zone). firewall-cmd --get-services (all predefined service names). firewall-cmd --info-service=http (what ports a service includes).

FRONT: How do you create a user account?
BACK: useradd USERNAME (creates user, home dir, group). Key options: -m (force create home dir), -s /bin/bash (set shell), -G wheel,developers (supplementary groups), -u 1500 (specific UID), -d /custom/home (custom home dir), -c 'Full Name' (comment).

FRONT: How do you modify an existing user account?
BACK: usermod -aG wheel user (add to supplementary group — MUST use -a or it replaces all groups). usermod -s /sbin/nologin user (disable login). usermod -L user (lock account). usermod -U user (unlock). usermod -d /new/home -m user (move home dir).

FRONT: How do you delete a user account?
BACK: userdel USERNAME (remove user, keep home dir and mail). userdel -r USERNAME (remove user AND home dir and mail spool). Always check for running processes first: ps -u USERNAME.

FRONT: How do you set and manage passwords?
BACK: passwd USERNAME (set password, root can change any). passwd -l USERNAME (lock). passwd -u USERNAME (unlock). passwd -e USERNAME (expire, forces change on next login). passwd -S USERNAME (show password status).

FRONT: How do you configure password aging with chage?
BACK: chage -l USERNAME (show aging info). chage -M 90 USERNAME (max days between changes). chage -m 7 USERNAME (min days between changes). chage -W 14 USERNAME (warning days before expiry). chage -E 2025-12-31 USERNAME (account expiration date).

FRONT: What are the fields in /etc/passwd?
BACK: username:x:UID:GID:comment:homedir:shell. 'x' means password is in /etc/shadow. UIDs: 0=root, 1-999=system, 1000+=regular users. /sbin/nologin prevents interactive login. Example: bob:x:1001:1001:Bob Smith:/home/bob:/bin/bash

FRONT: What are the fields in /etc/shadow?
BACK: username:password_hash:last_change:min:max:warn:inactive:expire:reserved. Password hash starts with $6$ (SHA-512), $y$ (yescrypt). !! or * means no password set (locked). last_change is days since Jan 1, 1970.

FRONT: How do you create and manage groups?
BACK: groupadd GROUPNAME (create). groupadd -g 2000 GROUPNAME (specific GID). groupmod -n NEWNAME OLDNAME (rename). groupdel GROUPNAME (delete, can't delete if it's a user's primary group). groups USERNAME shows group memberships.

FRONT: How do you manage group membership?
BACK: usermod -aG GROUP USER (add user to supplementary group). gpasswd -a USER GROUP (add). gpasswd -d USER GROUP (remove). gpasswd -M user1,user2 GROUP (set full membership list). id USERNAME (show UID, GID, and all groups).

FRONT: How do you configure sudo access?
BACK: visudo (safe edit of /etc/sudoers). Better: create files in /etc/sudoers.d/USERNAME. Syntax: user ALL=(ALL) ALL (full sudo). %wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL (group-based). user ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL (no password). Keep files chmod 440.

FRONT: What is the /etc/login.defs file?
BACK: System-wide defaults for user creation: PASS_MAX_DAYS (password max age), PASS_MIN_DAYS, PASS_MIN_LEN, PASS_WARN_AGE, UID_MIN/UID_MAX (range for new users), CREATE_HOME (yes/no), UMASK (default).

FRONT: What is umask and how does it work?
BACK: umask sets default permission bits to REMOVE from new files/dirs. Default umask 0022: files get 644 (666-022), dirs get 755 (777-022). umask 0077: files get 600, dirs get 700 (private). Set in /etc/bashrc or /etc/profile for persistence.

FRONT: How do you calculate permissions from a umask?
BACK: Files: start at 666 (no execute), subtract umask. Dirs: start at 777, subtract umask. umask 027: files=640 (rw-r-----), dirs=750 (rwxr-x---). umask 077: files=600, dirs=700. The umask never adds permissions, only removes.

FRONT: How do you generate an SSH key pair?
BACK: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 (modern, preferred) or ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 (legacy compatible). Creates ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (private) and ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (public). Protect private key with a passphrase.

FRONT: How do you set up SSH key-based authentication?
BACK: 1) ssh-keygen (generate keypair). 2) ssh-copy-id user@host (copies public key to remote ~/.ssh/authorized_keys). Or manually: append public key to remote ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. 3) Test: ssh user@host (should not prompt for password).

FRONT: What are the critical SSH file permissions?
BACK: ~/.ssh/ must be 700. ~/.ssh/authorized_keys must be 600. Private key must be 600. Public key can be 644. If permissions are wrong, SSH silently falls back to password auth. The remote user's home dir must not be group/world-writable.

FRONT: What sshd_config settings should you know?
BACK: PermitRootLogin yes/no/prohibit-password. PasswordAuthentication yes/no (disable for key-only). Port 22 (change if needed — update SELinux: semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp NEWPORT and firewalld). After changes: systemctl restart sshd.

FRONT: What are the three SELinux modes?
BACK: Enforcing: policy is enforced, violations are blocked and logged. Permissive: policy is not enforced, violations are only logged (for testing). Disabled: SELinux is completely off (requires reboot to re-enable and full relabel).

FRONT: How do you check and change the SELinux mode?
BACK: getenforce (show current mode). setenforce 0 (switch to permissive, temporary). setenforce 1 (switch to enforcing, temporary). For persistence: edit /etc/selinux/config → SELINUX=enforcing. Changes between disabled and enforcing require a reboot.

FRONT: What is an SELinux security context?
BACK: A label in the format user:role:type:level. Example: system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0. The type field is most important — Type Enforcement rules decide access based on the process type and file type.

FRONT: How do you view SELinux contexts on files and processes?
BACK: ls -Z (files). ps -Z (processes). id -Z (current user). stat FILE (includes context). Example: ls -Z /var/www/html/ shows httpd_sys_content_t. ps -Z | grep httpd shows httpd_t.

FRONT: How do you restore default SELinux file contexts?
BACK: restorecon -Rv /path (restore recursively, verbose). Use after moving files with mv (which preserves wrong labels) or after creating files in non-standard locations. restorecon reads the policy to determine correct labels.

FRONT: How do you add a custom SELinux file context rule?
BACK: semanage fcontext -a -t TYPE '/path(/.*)?'. Example: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/custom/www(/.*)?'. Then: restorecon -Rv /custom/www. The rule persists across relabels. List rules: semanage fcontext -l.

FRONT: How do you manage SELinux port labels?
BACK: semanage port -l (list all port labels). semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 (add port). semanage port -d -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 (delete). Required when running services on non-standard ports. Example: httpd on port 8443.

FRONT: How do you use SELinux booleans?
BACK: getsebool -a (list all booleans and values). setsebool httpd_enable_homedirs on (temporary). setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on (persistent, the -P flag is critical). Common: httpd_can_network_connect, samba_enable_home_dirs.

FRONT: What is the SELinux troubleshooting workflow?
BACK: 1) setenforce 0 to test if SELinux is the cause. 2) ausearch -m avc -ts recent (find denials in audit log). 3) audit2why < /var/log/audit/audit.log (explain why). 4) Fix with: restorecon (wrong label) → setsebool -P (boolean) → semanage (context/port rule).

FRONT: What is the most common SELinux file label mistake?
BACK: Using mv instead of cp. mv preserves the source label; cp inherits the destination directory's label. A file moved to /var/www/html/ keeps its old label (e.g., user_home_t) instead of getting httpd_sys_content_t. Fix: restorecon -Rv.

FRONT: How do you ensure all configurations persist after reboot?
BACK: Use --permanent with firewall-cmd (then --reload). Use systemctl enable for services. Mount entries go in /etc/fstab (run systemctl daemon-reload). SELinux: setsebool -P, /etc/selinux/config. nmcli changes are persistent by default. Cron/at are persistent by default.

FRONT: What is the difference between systemctl enable and systemctl start?
BACK: start activates a service NOW but it won't survive reboot. enable sets it to start at boot but doesn't start it now. Use enable --now to do both. This distinction is critical for the RHCSA — the exam requires persistence.

FRONT: How do you find which package provides a specific file?
BACK: dnf provides /path/to/file or dnf provides '*/filename'. Example: dnf provides /usr/sbin/semanage finds policycoreutils-python-utils. Useful when a command is missing and you need to install the right package.

FRONT: How do you use nmcli to configure a connection with DHCP?
BACK: nmcli con add type ethernet con-name dhcp-conn ifname eth0 ipv4.method auto. This is the default — NetworkManager uses DHCP to obtain IP, gateway, and DNS. nmcli con up dhcp-conn to activate.

FRONT: What is the difference between nmcli con down and nmcli dev disconnect?
BACK: nmcli con down CONN deactivates a connection profile (another profile on the same device may auto-activate). nmcli dev disconnect DEV disconnects the device entirely, preventing any auto-activation. Use dev disconnect for a clean takedown.

FRONT: How do you create a swap partition using LVM?
BACK: lvcreate -L 2G -n swaplv myvg → mkswap /dev/myvg/swaplv → swapon /dev/myvg/swaplv → add to /etc/fstab: /dev/myvg/swaplv swap swap defaults 0 0 → systemctl daemon-reload. Verify: swapon --show.

FRONT: What does 'non-destructively' mean for the RHCSA storage objectives?
BACK: Add new storage (partitions, LVs, swap) without unmounting existing filesystems, losing data, or rebooting. Use fdisk to add partitions to free space, partprobe to reload, and extend LVs while mounted.

FRONT: How do you list all block devices and their filesystems?
BACK: lsblk -f shows NAME, FSTYPE, LABEL, UUID, MOUNTPOINT for all block devices. blkid shows similar info in a flat list. Both are essential for identifying devices before mounting or adding to fstab.

FRONT: How do you troubleshoot a system that won't boot due to a bad /etc/fstab entry?
BACK: Boot to emergency mode (systemd.unit=emergency.target at GRUB). Mount root read-write: mount -o remount,rw /. Edit /etc/fstab: fix or comment out the bad entry. Run systemctl daemon-reload. Reboot. Tip: add nofail to fstab entries for non-critical mounts.

FRONT: What does the nofail mount option do in /etc/fstab?
BACK: nofail tells systemd not to fail the boot if this filesystem can't be mounted (e.g., NFS server is down, USB drive not plugged in). Without it, a failed mount entry halts the boot into emergency mode.

FRONT: How do you configure a DHCP connection for IPv4 and a static IPv6 address?
BACK: nmcli con mod CONN ipv4.method auto ipv6.method manual ipv6.addresses 'fd00::10/64' ipv6.gateway 'fd00::1'. nmcli con up CONN. Verify: ip addr show and ip -6 route show.

FRONT: How do you use tar to back up and restore with permissions intact?
BACK: Backup: tar --selinux --acls --xattrs -czpf /backup/etc.tar.gz /etc. The -p flag preserves permissions. Restore: tar --selinux --acls --xattrs -xzpf /backup/etc.tar.gz -C /. Critical for RHCSA where SELinux contexts must survive.

FRONT: What happens if you change /etc/selinux/config from enforcing to disabled?
BACK: SELinux is fully disabled after reboot. To re-enable: set SELINUX=enforcing in the config, then reboot. The system will auto-relabel all files on boot (slow, can take 10+ minutes). Avoid disabling SELinux on the exam.

FRONT: How do you check for SELinux denials in the audit log?
BACK: ausearch -m avc -ts recent (recent denials). ausearch -m avc -c httpd (specific to httpd). grep AVC /var/log/audit/audit.log. sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log (if setroubleshoot is installed, gives human-readable explanations).

FRONT: What is the purpose of the /etc/sudoers.d/ directory?
BACK: Drop-in files for sudo configuration. Files here are included by /etc/sudoers via #includedir. Easier to manage than editing /etc/sudoers directly — each user or role gets its own file. Files must have no dots in the name and be chmod 440.

FRONT: How do you lock and expire a user account?
BACK: Lock (prevent login): usermod -L user (adds ! to password hash) or passwd -l user. Expire (set expiration date): chage -E 0 user (expire immediately) or usermod -e 2025-12-31 user. Unexpire: chage -E -1 user.

FRONT: What is the difference between /sbin/nologin and locking an account?
BACK: /sbin/nologin (usermod -s /sbin/nologin) prevents interactive login but allows services to run as the user. Locking (usermod -L) adds '!' to the password hash, blocking password auth but not SSH key auth. Use both for full lockout.

FRONT: How do you find all files owned by a specific user or group?
BACK: find / -user USERNAME (by user). find / -group GROUPNAME (by group). find / -nouser (files with no matching user in /etc/passwd — orphaned files). find / -nogroup (no matching group). Useful for cleanup after deleting a user.

FRONT: How do you use systemctl edit to override a unit file?
BACK: systemctl edit SERVICE creates a drop-in override in /etc/systemd/system/SERVICE.d/override.conf. Only add the sections/directives you want to change. systemctl edit --full SERVICE copies the entire unit for full editing. Then: systemctl daemon-reload.

FRONT: What is the difference between rescue.target and emergency.target?
BACK: rescue.target: mounts all local filesystems, starts some services, gives a root shell. Like single-user mode. emergency.target: mounts only root filesystem (read-only), starts almost nothing. For when rescue.target fails.

FRONT: How do you verify NFS mounts are working?
BACK: showmount -e SERVER (list server's exports). mount -t nfs SERVER:/share /mnt/test (test mount). df -hT (verify mount and filesystem type). For autofs: ls /mnt/auto/share (triggers automount), mount | grep nfs (verify).

FRONT: What are the key systemd timer features vs cron?
BACK: Timers: can depend on boot time (OnBootSec=), support randomized delay (RandomizedDelaySec=), catch up after downtime (Persistent=true), per-unit logging via journalctl, and don't need a separate daemon. Cron: simpler syntax, widely known, runs via crond service.

FRONT: How do you check if a service failed and view its logs?
BACK: systemctl status SERVICE (shows state and recent log lines). systemctl --failed (list all failed units). journalctl -u SERVICE -p err (error-level logs for that unit). journalctl -u SERVICE --since '10 min ago' (recent logs).

FRONT: How do you boot, reboot, and shut down a system?
BACK: systemctl reboot (reboot). systemctl poweroff (power off). shutdown -h now (halt immediately). shutdown -r +5 "message" (reboot in 5 minutes with wall message). shutdown -c (cancel pending shutdown). All equivalent to legacy reboot/halt/poweroff commands.

FRONT: What is grubby and when do you use it?
BACK: grubby is the primary tool on RHEL for managing per-kernel boot parameters via BLS entries in /boot/loader/entries/. Use grubby for kernel args; use grub2-mkconfig for global GRUB settings (timeout, console). grubby edits are immediate — no regeneration step needed.

FRONT: How do you add and remove kernel parameters with grubby?
BACK: grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="console=ttyS0" (add to all kernels). grubby --update-kernel=ALL --remove-args="rhgb quiet" (remove). grubby --info=ALL (show all kernel entries). grubby --default-kernel (show default). grubby --set-default-index=0 (set default).

FRONT: What does lvextend -r do?
BACK: lvextend -r (or --resizefs) extends the logical volume AND resizes the filesystem in one command. Example: lvextend -r -L +500M /dev/myvg/mylv. Automatically detects XFS vs ext4 and calls xfs_growfs or resize2fs for you. Saves a step on the exam.

FRONT: How do you ensure a NetworkManager connection starts automatically at boot?
BACK: nmcli con mod CONN connection.autoconnect yes. This is the default for new connections but worth verifying. nmcli con mod CONN connection.autoconnect no prevents auto-activation. Check with: nmcli -f connection.autoconnect con show CONN.

FRONT: How do you list active systemd timers?
BACK: systemctl list-timers (show active timers with next/last fire times). systemctl list-timers --all (include inactive). Use this to verify your timer is scheduled correctly after enabling it.

FRONT: How do you set a filesystem label and mount by label?
BACK: XFS: umount first, then xfs_admin -L "mylabel" /dev/sdX1. ext4: e2label /dev/sdX1 "mylabel" (or tune2fs -L). Then in /etc/fstab: LABEL=mylabel /mnt/data xfs defaults 0 0. Verify: blkid shows LABEL, lsblk -f shows LABEL column.

FRONT: What is nmtui?
BACK: A text-based user interface for NetworkManager. Run nmtui to get a menu for editing connections, activating connections, and setting the hostname. Useful as a fallback if you forget nmcli syntax on the exam.
